extracted.intended_audience: television/culture readers and comedy critics (general readers interested in SNL and sketch comedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the quality and appropriateness of a televised sketch (here: an SNL skit) with emphasis on handling sensitive subjects and conveying satirical intent. Focuses on tone, target clarity, originality, and audience reception for televised satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of satirical intent
rubrics_metrics.description: "It's unclear whether the core comedic conceit of the episode was intended to be taken at face value or whether SNL was attempting to parody the kind of person who thinks it's not child abuse if the abuser happens to be a voluptuous female.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the piece is intended as parody, the target and critical stance must be communicated clearly; ambiguity risks the audience reading the sketch as endorsement rather than critique. Signal intent through context, framing, and punchline construction; avoid subtlety that leaves the impression you’re celebrating the problematic attitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical bite (sharpness of critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: "SNL managed to parrot South Park's Sgt. Yates — the cop who responds to similar allegations by quipping 'nice!' — without any of the satirical bite.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire should have a detectable edge or critical consequence; mere imitation of an offensive trope without incisive commentary fails. Provide targets, consequences, or framing that make the critique evident rather than repeating an offensive gag for shock or cheap laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mocking victims
rubrics_metrics.description: "the sketch wasn't just unfunny — it was mocking the victims of child rape.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never make victims the butt of jokes about their own abuse. Anti-patterns include celebrating the abuser’s attractiveness, treating victimization as punchline material, or producing humor that trivializes trauma. If the humor references victims, it must clearly condemn the harm rather than minimize it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cheap/tasteless 'low-hanging fruit' jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: "frat bro-style snickering over the attractiveness of an accused child molester is really, really low-hanging fruit.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of easy, base jokes (sexualization, leering, frat-bro snickering) that rely on shock or prurience instead of wit. If the only comedic mechanism is awkward sexualization or juvenile snickering, the sketch should be rethought or killed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject suitability / moral boundary consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: "it's probably a good general rule to steer clear of things like child molestation if the joke is essentially creepy leering.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While satire can address morally repulsive topics, creators should weigh whether a subject is suitable for comedic treatment and whether the approach is responsible. Sensitive subjects require clear purpose, ethical framing, and a demonstrable critical angle; absent that, avoid tackling them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and overall comfort level
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sketch — ... has a few funny lines, but its overall bent is more than a little uncomfortable.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the cumulative tone produces purposeful discomfort (with clear commentary) or merely makes viewers uneasy. Discomfort as a tool must be justified by satirical intent or insight; otherwise it signals poor comedic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and not parroting problematic tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Gothamist compared the sketch to a bad Adam Sandler movie... SNL managed to parrot South Park's Sgt. Yates...",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid recycling tired, problematic jokes from other sources without adding new perspective or critique. Rehashing well-known offensive tropes risks dilution of satire and invites criticism; strive for a fresh angle that interrogates, not repeats, the trope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience expectation and entertainment value
rubrics_metrics.description: "At a time when SNL seems to be recovering from a long stretch of unfunny seasons and general malaise, viewers were probably hoping for something a little more entertaining than a 15-year-old who thinks rape is hilarious.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the show's current momentum and audience expectations: satire should still deliver entertainment and payoff. If a sketch undermines audience trust or satisfaction—especially during a perceived recovery period—it can damage reception; balance provocation with craft and comedic reward.
